title: Probability: Compound Events, Tree Diagrams and Two-Way Tables
seo_title: Grade 9 Probability Worksheets with Answers (CAPS Maths)
standard_text: Consider situations with equally probable outcomes; determine probabilities for compound events using two-way tables and tree diagrams; determine the probabilities for outcomes of events and predict their relative frequency in simple experiments; compare relative frequency with probability and explain possible differences.
meta_desc: Free CAPS Grade 9 probability worksheets: single and complementary events, two dice, sample spaces, Venn diagrams and two-way tables. 100 questions with memos.
key_sub: List outcomes in a table or tree.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • Probability = favourable outcomes ÷ all equally likely outcomes.
  • P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
  • For two events, list the outcomes in a table or tree diagram.
  • In a Venn diagram, count the overlap only once.

Examples

Example

Two coins: at least one head

HH, HT, TH, TT

3 of 4

Answer: 3/4

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Adding instead of listingList the outcomes.
Missing outcomesUse a table or tree.
The overlap twiceCount it once.

items.q: Two fair dice are rolled and the scores are subtracted (larger − smaller). What is the probability of a difference less than 2?
items.e: Draw a 6 × 6 sample space: 36 equally likely outcomes. 16 of them give a difference less than 2, so P = 1636 = 49.

items.e: Draw a 6 × 6 sample space: 36 equally likely outcomes. 1 of them gives a product of 25, so P = 136.

items.q: Two fair dice are rolled and the scores are added. What is the probability of a total of 12?
items.e: There are 36 outcomes. A total of 12 comes from (6; 6): 1 way, so P = 136.

items.q: Two fair dice are rolled and the scores are added. What is the probability of a total of 9?
items.e: There are 36 outcomes. A total of 9 comes from (3; 6), (4; 5), (5; 4), (6; 3): 4 ways, so P = 436 = 19.

items.q: A fair dice is rolled 300 times. How many times would you expect to get a 6?
items.e: Expected number = probability × number of trials = 16 × 300 = 50.

items.q: A coin is flipped and a fair dice is rolled. How many possible outcomes are there?
items.e: 2 outcomes for the coin × 6 for the dice = 12.

items.q: A fair dice is rolled 60 times. How many times would you expect to get a 6?
items.e: Expected number = probability × number of trials = 16 × 60 = 10.

items.q: Two fair dice are rolled and the scores are added. What is the probability of a total of 4?
items.e: There are 36 outcomes. A total of 4 comes from (1; 3), (2; 2), (3; 1): 3 ways, so P = 336 = 112.

items.q: Two fair dice are rolled and the scores are added. What is the probability of a total of 7?
items.e: There are 36 outcomes. A total of 7 comes from (1; 6), (2; 5), (3; 4), (4; 3), (5; 2), (6; 1): 6 ways, so P = 636 = 16.

items.q: Three coins are flipped. What is the probability of getting three heads?
items.e: There are 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 outcomes and only HHH works: 18.

items.q: A fair dice is rolled 300 times. How many times would you expect to get an even number?
items.e: Expected number = probability × number of trials = 12 × 300 = 150.

items.q: Two coins are flipped. What is the probability of getting one head and one tail?
items.e: Outcomes: HH, HT, TH, TT. Two of the four work (HT and TH): 12.
